claims.text: Precise control over synthesis cooling rate and thermal history promotes favorable local atomic ordering in noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials.
Favorable local atomic ordering minimizes local strain.
Controlled thermal history optimizes the mixing enthalpy among the constituent noble metals.
Local ordering, minimized strain, and optimized mixing enthalpy promote reliable formation of uniform catalytic active sites.
Uniform catalytic active sites produced by controlled thermal history improve catalytic performance.
At temperatures below the constituent metals' melting points, sufficient controlled diffusion can occur to form ordered local arrangements.
Optimized intermetallic distances promote synergistic electronic interactions.
Gradual atomic rearrangement during controlled thermal treatment reduces local atomic mismatch and strain.
Mixing enthalpy governs the specific local ordering pattern produced during controlled thermal treatment.
The resulting ordering produces a uniform distribution of catalytic active sites that enhances reaction kinetics.
Slow-annealed HEA nanomaterials will have more uniform nanoparticle composition than rapidly quenched materials.
Slow-annealed HEA nanomaterials will have a narrower particle-size distribution than rapidly quenched materials.
Slow-annealed HEA nanomaterials will show sharper XRD peaks than rapidly quenched materials.
Slow-annealed HEA nanomaterials will exhibit higher catalytic turnover frequencies than rapidly quenched materials.
Rapid quenching kinetically traps greater compositional disorder and local strain.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold below alloy melting points, under inert atmospheres with minimized oxidation, and for reactions sensitive to surface electronic structure.
Hydrogen evolution and oxygen reduction are examples of reactions sensitive to the electronic structure of surface active sites.
The optimization window for temperature and cooling rate is uncertain.
The role of electronic-structure changes caused by subtle local ordering has not been fully established for specific catalytic reactions.
